newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada sees little need for more easing.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada sees little need for more easing.

text.p: The Bank of Canada said on Thursday that it did not see the need for further monetary easing if the economy and inflation developed as predicted.

"In the absence of unexpected developments in inflation or economic activity, the possible need for further monetary easing...has largely disappeared," the bank said in its semi-annual Monetary Policy Report released on Thursday.
"Over the medium term, as slack in the economy is absorbed, the bank will need to promote less stimulative monetary conditions in order to maintain Canada's low trend of inflation," the bank said.
The central bank said that recent economic momentum "significantly reduced" the risk of inflation falling below the bank's target range of one to three percent.
Canada's economy was expected to grow vigorously throughout 1997, boosted by external demand and an expected rise in domestic spending, the report said.
But the bank said the amount of slack remaining in the Canadian economy would hold back price pressures, keeping inflation in the lower half of the inflation target band.
The bank estimated that the slack in the economy, or output gap, narrowed in the second half of 1996 to 2.5 percent by the end of the year.

"Overall, the margin of unused capacity in the economy, combined with rising productivity and highly competitive global markets, continued to exert downward pressure on prices and costs," the bank said.
The central bank said it expected to see "significant momentum" into the second half of 1997, sustained by the monetary easing fostered by the Bank of Canada last year.

"The bank thus continues to expect average growth ot around four percent through to the fourth quarter of 1997, which should translate into annual growth of somewhat less than four percent for the year," the report said.
The bank also said it was keeping a close watch on the growth of M1, the narrow measure of money in Canada.
The growth of M1 picked up speed in the past six months, pointing to strong economic activity in the next few quarters, the bank said.
"However, if such rapid growth in M1 were to persist into 1998, it would not be consistent with preserving low inflation," the bank said. "Accordingly, M1 growth will require close monitoring."
A temporary increase in M1 growth was consistent with a return of the Canadian economy to full capacity, the central bank said.
The bank said the rate of increase of broad monetary aggregates remained moderate.

With the Canadian economy picking up speed, the challenge for the bank now is to foster monetary conditions that "support a durable expansion and preserve Canada's low rate of inflation," the report said.
The Bank of Canada said the recent volatility of the Canadian dollar and short and medium-term interest rates was linked to a rate hike in March by the U.S. Federal Reserve.

But the bank said that despite the volatility, Canadian financial markets continued to be supported by strong fundamentals: low inflation, declining net public borrowing and an improved external balance of payments.

Those factors had led to a large decrease in the risk premiums attached to Canadian assets, the bank said, "and they continue to underpin market expectations of a future appreciation of the Canadian dollar."
The release of the report prompted little change in trading of Canadian bonds, T-bills and the currency.
((Reuters Ottawa Bureau 613 235-6745))
